title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is one of training-data sourcing: an AI music generation system was deployed to millions of users while allegedly built on copyrighted recordings obtained without the rights holders' permission or compensation. The problem did not emerge from a single edge case but from the foundational data decisions made before the product launched. It surfaced publicly through output, specifically generated audio close enough to existing recordings that major labels could point to specific tracks as evidence.

This is a system-used-outside-the-conditions-it-was-built-for failure only in the narrowest sense. More precisely, it is a case where the conditions under which it was built were themselves the problem: the training corpus allegedly incorporated protected works without licensing agreements. A licensing review of training data before deployment would have been the point at which this could have been caught. No such review, or none adequate to the scale alleged, appears to have occurred.

The lawsuits are allegations, not findings, and no court has yet ruled on whether Udio's training practices constituted infringement. What is established is that settlements were reached with some plaintiffs, that Sony filed a separate suit asserting more than 30,000 additional recordings, that an independent artists' class action survived a dismissal motion, and that a musicians' union also filed a related lawsuit against a label that settled with Udio.

summary:
# Summary

Universal Music Group and AI music startup Udio have reached a settlement, ending a lawsuit that accused Udio of using copyrighted music to train its artificial intelligence system. UMG, along with Sony Music and Warner Music Group, had sued Udio for allegedly creating songs similar to popular hits without permission or compensation, including a track resembling The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the agreement, Udio will launch a new platform next year trained only on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed.

Udio, founded in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including musician will.i.am and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will compensate artists who opt into the new platform. The settlement marks Udio's first music licensing deal with a major label. Meanwhile, UMG also announced a partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers. Millions of users have accessed Udio since its launch, with approximately 128,000 app downloads since May.
